prize_parts.citation: For showing how collateral constraints and financial frictions amplify and propagate shocks, giving macroeconomics a theory of credit cycles and of the role of balance sheets in financial intermediation.

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) gave a tractable account of how collateral values and borrowing limits feed back on each other and turn small shocks into persistent downturns. This is the macro counterpart of what we know from financial contracting: when claims on future cash flows cannot be pledged in full, asset prices and credit availability become part of the transmission mechanism. Gertler's work, including the later work on financial intermediaries with Kiyotaki, moves the idea from stylised models into quantitative macro and shows how disruption in intermediary balance sheets can drive aggregate fluctuations and shape policy responses. The framework has been used, tested and extended for roughly three decades, and the 2008 crisis and its aftermath confirmed its relevance. It is conceptually original, and its influence on research, central-bank modelling and financial regulation is broad. Colleagues' openings place it high on both merit and maturity: four members rank it first or second, and no one questions that the timing is ripe. That matters most to me, because several competing candidates are younger.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with the 2022 prize for work on banks and financial crises. Bernanke's recognition covers part of the accelerator and balance-sheet territory, which weakens the case for crediting Gertler, and Gertler also appears on B015. A Kiyotaki-Moore pair is cleaner on attribution but gives up the quantitative and intermediary strand. Another concern is that the evidence for the mechanism is more often indirect or calibrated than cleanly identified, and Gilchrist's empirical work is left out under the three-name cap. Finally, B002 and B027 have broader first-place support, and I should not wave that away. I do not treat it as scientific merit, though, and it does not change my own assessment.

responses.point: Hassler sees Kiyotaki-Moore as a clear two-person core and considers a narrower prize natural, since Bernanke's 2022 award partly covers the financial-accelerator strand. He is unsure whether Gertler should be added as a third laureate.
responses.response: I agree that the pair is the cleanest unit and that the Bernanke overlap is a real cost, as my own opening noted. I still keep Gertler, for a narrower reason than the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator. His later work with Kiyotaki on intermediary balance sheets in quantitative macro models is a separate step, and it is the channel through which the mechanism entered post-2008 policy analysis. If the Committee judges the 2022 prize to have exhausted the accelerator territory, the Kiyotaki-Moore pair is a defensible fallback, and I would not object strongly to it. I would want that choice made on the attribution argument, not just on the wish for a smaller prize.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B004 seventh. She accepts that Kiyotaki and Moore are the clear originators and that the mechanism became central after the crisis, but notes that empirical identification is indirect and that overlap with the Bernanke recognition and with Gertler's New Keynesian candidacy diffuses credit.
responses.response: The point on identification is fair, and it is the part of the case I take most seriously. The mechanism is hard to test cleanly at the aggregate level. Yet the underlying logic, that pledgeable collateral limits investment and borrowing, is the same logic that corporate-finance and credit-market studies at the firm and household level have examined for years. I draw that from my general knowledge of the literature, not from anything I have checked here. So I see the evidence as cumulative and varied in design, not just calibrated. I agree the diffusion of Gertler's credit across B004 and B015 is a real issue. It is why I would credit him here only for the intermediary-finance strand.

responses.point: Dreber-Almenberg ranks B002 first. She argues that population-scale administrative data created a new empirical standard, that the core results have been widely replicated or extended, and that the policy impact is very large. She also flags strong identifying assumptions behind the causal place-effect claims.
responses.response: I agree with much of this, and I placed B002 sixth mainly on maturity, not on quality. The data infrastructure and the descriptive facts on mobility look durable. My hesitation concerns the causal interpretation of neighbourhood and exposure effects, which your own uncertainties also flag, and the difficulty of dividing credit across a large team. I would not argue that B002 is unworthy. I think it is a strong candidate that the Committee could reasonably prefer now or later, which is why I list it as an alternative. What I resist is letting the number of members who put it first stand in for the open question on long-run causal claims.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B027 first. He argues that political economics built a formal and empirical framework for constitutions, electoral rules and state capacity, with a mature record and a well-defined trio of Persson, Tabellini and Besley. He notes the overlap with the 2024 institutions prize and the weaker cross-country identification of some electoral-rule effects.
responses.response: I agree that B027 has among the cleanest attribution structures on the shortlist, and I ranked it third for that reason. The work is mature, and the credit is concentrated in the Persson-Tabellini synthesis and the Besley-Persson state-capacity work. My reservations are the two you identify. The 2024 prize is adjacent in theme, and the cross-country empirical identification is less clean than the theory. I would not want to discount the field because it is political economy, and I treat it on the same footing as the macro-finance candidate. I keep it as an alternative, not my preferred configuration, because I put somewhat more weight on the breadth of the macro-financial mechanism and its policy use.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee regards the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises as having already covered the financial-friction agenda, and whether a Kiyotaki-Moore pair is therefore cleaner than the trio.
Whether Gertler's intermediary-finance contribution can be separated from the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator credit and from his role on B015.
How much weight to give a mechanism whose aggregate evidence is mostly indirect or calibrated, and whether Gilchrist's empirical work should be credited.
Whether the long-run causal evidence on B002 and the 2024-prize overlap on B027 should change the relative ordering of these candidates.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile: no listed co-author or institutional connection with Kiyotaki, Moore or Gertler. My research on financial contracting and incomplete-contracts theory is adjacent to the collateral-constraint literature, and I chaired the Committee in 2016-2018, so familiarity with that field may bias my assessment. I disclose this and do not adjudicate it.
